text: Lesson 13 stood up the log destination monitoring depends on. The natural next instinct is to alert on everything the platform now makes visible — every metric, every threshold. That instinct is wrong. A metric existing doesn't mean a deviation in it matters, and an alert nobody needs to act on just teaches people to ignore alerts. The real skill is picking the small number of alerts that correspond to something a person genuinely needs to know about.

Almost every alert worth having for a new deployment falls into one of three buckets. Resource thresholds — CPU, memory, and disk crossing a level that actually threatens availability, not just a level that's merely elevated. Failed health checks — a load balancer probe or an instance status check saying the resource stopped responding. And security-relevant events — repeated failed sign-ins or an unexpected change to a network security group, worth a look regardless of resource load.

A basic deployment genuinely needs about four alerts to start. Sustained high CPU, above 85% for 15 minutes, catching a runaway process rather than a brief normal spike. Low disk free space, below 15%, catching the exact failure mode from Lesson 13's disk example with time to act. A failed health check, meaning the instance is unreachable right now. And repeated failed authentication attempts, a security signal worth a human look. That's a deliberately short list.

An alert rule by itself only evaluates a condition — it still needs somewhere to send the notification. Azure uses an Action Group, email, SMS, or a webhook, attached to the alert rule. AWS uses an SNS topic that a CloudWatch Alarm publishes to, with subscribers on the other end. Either way, the alert and the notification are two separate pieces wired together, and an alert with no notification attached is exactly as useless as no alert at all.

Four alerts, each earning its place, each tied to a real notification — that's the starting set for this environment. Next up: why setting thresholds too sensitively right from day one guarantees a flood of noise that trains people to ignore every alert this chapter just configured.
